articles.title_orig: Russia, Ukraine agree to Oleshky ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump, White House says
articles.title_zh: Russia, Ukraine agree to Oleshky ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump, White House says
articles.content_orig:
People in Russian-occupied city facing severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with some reportedly surviving on weeds
The White House said on Friday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.
In a statement, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 29 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians. Moscow and Kyiv are yet to comment on the developments.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.
The statement said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump, and her representative worked directly with ​Russian and Ukrainian ‌leadership to define the ​terms.
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” Melania Trump said.
Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network , despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.
The slowdown, which has affected the key communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Starlink founder Musk publicly criticised Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with both Trump and Musk denying responsibility.
“I don’t comment one way or the other,” Trump said on Thursday when asked about reports that he had personally called Musk to demand the restrictions be lifted.
“The bottom line: he put it back.”
But Ukrainian officials said on Friday morning that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.
“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.
“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.
The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering both offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.
after newsletter promotion
The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, have plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.
Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel , as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.
Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.
Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war.
“The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.
The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

articles.title_orig: New for Necromunda in 2027
articles.title_zh: New for Necromunda in 2027
articles.content_orig:
New for Necromunda in 2027
There’s an exciting year ahead for fans of Necromunda, with a lineup more stuffed than the questionably-sourced contents of a back-alley Scabber’s overcoat. There will be new miniatures, new terrain, new vehicles and new expansions. However, there won’t be a Roleplay expansion.
After careful consideration we’ve decided to focus our efforts on providing even more great minis for the core game.
Don’t worry – all the minis we showcased in the Big Autumn Preview are still on their way, and will be available for use in standard games of Necromunda.
Looking ahead to 2027, the new releases will cover multiple key gangs and locations, so here's a roadmap, because everybody loves roadmaps.*
Starting in the spring, we go back to the ash wastes with new rules expansions and the biggest plastic vehicle kit yet released for Necromunda.
Then, those brave enough can once more enter the cursed depths of the Underhells in search of ancient archeotech, where among other things they will bump into new Fighters for the Malstrain Genestealer cults.
And then we return to the still-smoking urban sprawl of Cinderak City, one of the conflict flashpoints of the recent Aranthian Succession . This is accompanied by support for some of the original underhive crews of Necromunda, including hulking new brutes.
And we’re still not done for 2027. Rounding out the year, there will be new mercenaries and gunslingers, set on hunting down their unfortunate bounties in whatever dank or irradiated corner of Necromunda they sought to hide.
Alongside all of the above, you’ll also get support for other gangs, scenery, and regular rules expansions.
And still set to arrive this year is a major expansion for the House of Iron in the shape of three flexible new multipart plastic kits, offering an enormous range of new cosmetic and wargear options for your Orlock gang.
We’ll cover them all in more detail soon, so check back regularly, and sign up to the Warhammer newsletter to stay up to date with the latest Necromunda news.
* Everybody except the Ash Waste Nomads, but they just hate roads!

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Weil Gotshal Bleeds More Top Lawyers as It Holds Merger Talks
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Weil Gotshal Bleeds More Top Lawyers as It Holds Merger Talks
articles.content_orig:
Weil Gotshal & Manges and Willkie Farr & Gallagher have ended discussions over a possible merger, intensifying pressure on Weilâs leaders as many of its top partners take jobs elsewhere.
The talks were ended last night after the two sides had signed a non-disclosure agreement to discuss a tieup, two people familiar with the matter said. Willkie was the law firm Bloomberg Law reported Weil was in discussions with earlier this week.
On Thursday, at least some top partners at Weil had been holding discussions with their colleagues to build excitement for the possible tie-up, according to a person familiar with those discussions. By the end of the day, the merger talks were off.
The development came as more Weil partners headed for the exits.
The co-managing partner of Weilâs corporate department, Lyuba Goltser, plans to join Sidley Austin, according to a person familiar with the move. Davis Polk & Wardwell plans to bring on appellate litigator Drew Tulumello, another person said. And the Wall Street Journal reported Paul Weiss is hiring securities litigation partner Caroline Zalka. Tulumello and Zalka are members of Weilâs management committee.
It is unclear if Weil has lined up merger discussions with other firms, or whether its leaders will seek to do so. But continued departures of top partners risks setting off a so-called talent run, where partners begin to leave not because they can do better financially at another firm, but because they fear being left behind at a depleted firm.
âLateral movement for âI can do betterâ is very common,â said David McGowan, a law professor at the University of San Diego. âAnd the run on the bank metaphor happens when âI can do betterâ reaches a scale at which it turns into âI donât want to be left holding the bag.ââ
Some previous law firm mergers have come together after discussions broke down with early suitors.
Shearman & Sterling broke off talks with Hogan Lovells in 2023 before tying up with Allen & Overy. Kaye Scholer and Arnold & Porter in 2016 reportedly ended discussions, only for the talks to revive and the firms to merge.
Spokespeople for Weil and Willkie did not respond to requests for comment.
Large law firms in the US and UK have been actively exploring mergers in a race to scale and hot market for high-end corporate partners. A Weil combination with Willkie would have created a massive firm with more than $4 billion in annual revenue, placing it among the five largest based in the US.
Weil has been rocked by a string of partner departures in recent weeks, with more expected to be formally announced. The departures include Michael Aiello, the powerful corporate department leader who in September announced he would leave for Cravath, Swaine & Moore.

articles.title_orig: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
articles.title_zh: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
articles.content_orig:
People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans
J ack Price joined the marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on the meter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.
Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”
For generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting for less than 10% of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.
According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is $765 for a new car and $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay $1,000 or more a month , according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.
For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”
Y2K cars don’t encompass everything produced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect become mortgage payments on wheels – they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.
The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunk from 21% of inventory a year ago to 15% , according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”
On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlander with a screwdriver . “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”
In a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.
At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access to owners and even independent mechanics . Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.
Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ’em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”
Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘ What is going on?’” Price says. “The fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”
T wenty-five miles north-west of downtown Atlanta, a half hour’s drive in optimistic traffic, sits Town Center at Cobb, a typical suburban mall in recession. But on the first Sunday of every month, the mall parking comes alive for Caffeine and Octane, a sprawling car show that’s open to the public, free to attend and also has long lines for coffee and donut trucks. And even though the usual turnout of 2,000-plus cars was winnowed down to a few hundred on the gray, showery morning of October’s show, it was still an impressive array of vintage American muscle, Japanese domestic market (or JDM) unicorns and multimillion-dollar exotics. The Y2K cars stood out, too.
Sitting right at the entrance of the show was Anthony DeNaples’s 2000 Buick Regal GS, a sleeper sedan that has become a cult classic. He bought it four months ago for $18,000 on Facebook Marketplace, a price he considered a bargain for such a rare commuter. “Person didn’t really know what they had,” says the 37-year-old custom car builder, who uses the car to ferry his two young daughters. His oldest is constantly goading him to do burnouts, which she calls “making stripes”. Modern cars, he reasons, have become so laden with safety systems – for keeping the car in lane, or slamming on the brakes when sensors detect an obstacle – that they’re less fun to drive hard. “A lot of newer cars, if you want to drive it how it’s meant to be driven,

articles.title_orig: SK Hynix Stock Jumps After Scrapping U.S. IPO of Memory-Chip Unit
articles.title_zh: SK Hynix Stock Jumps After Scrapping U.S. IPO of Memory-Chip Unit
articles.content_orig:
Shares of South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix closed higher on Friday, reversing losses of as much as 3% earlier in the session after the company's decision to halt a review of a potential U.S. initial public offering for its subsidiary Solidigm.
The stock reversed earlier losses to close 4.4% higher.
Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, said the stock's rebound suggested that concerns over a potential Solidigm IPO had been weighing on investor sentiment.
"SK Hynix shareholders have got the outcome they were pushing for," Gilbert said, adding that "in the short term, it removes a governance worry and keeps Solidigm's value inside the company."
He explained that SK Hynix faces the challenge of funding Solidigm's growth without compromising share buybacks and dividends, as the company needs to demonstrate a credible funding plan as it prepares to report earnings next week.
"Solidigm will halt its review of potential pre-IPO and IPO options," the company said in the statement after assessing recent capital market conditions and share price trends, while also exploring various funding options to finance a new U.S. semiconductor fabrication plant amid growing demand for AI memory.
The chip manufacturer said an IPO could have helped fund Solidigm's expansion while providing greater financial flexibility for shareholder returns, including dividends, share buybacks and share cancellations.
However, financial market volatility had increased and contributed to a broader correction in semiconductor stocks, prompting SK Hynix to reassess whether an IPO would benefit existing shareholders.
SK Hynix said that Solidigm's existing production facilities had limited capacity to meet rising AI-driven memory demand, underscoring the need for additional manufacturing capacity in the U.S.
The decision also follows regulatory scrutiny in South Korea.
The country's financial regulator said Monday that a potential U.S. listing of Solidigm could violate South Korean rules restricting dual listings, according to Reuters.
Financial Supervisory Service Governor Lee Chan-jin said regulators were examining whether the IPO would require a review under the country's rules designed to protect minority shareholders.
SK Hynix said Solidigm's investment needs remain unchanged and that it would continue exploring alternative financing options to support the subsidiary's growth and enhance shareholder value.
The announcement comes as U.S. technology stocks face pressure amid worries over AI spending.The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 2.6% on Thursday, its worst session since June, while Nvidia fell 4.4% and Advanced Micro Devices dropped 8.1%.
Amid a sell-off in memory stocks, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that he does not expect an oversupply of memory chips by 2029, despite concerns over weakening demand.
AI data center stocks have also come under pressure amid growing concerns over financing risks and the pace of AI infrastructure expansion. Shares of CoreWeave plunged 10% on Thursday, extending their monthly decline to 36%, while Australia's NextDC tumbled nearly 40% on Wednesday after cutting its earnings forecast.

articles.title_orig: 'We're Victims of Xbox's Change in Strategy': Dishonored Dev Has Weeks to Save Itself
articles.title_zh: 'We're Victims of Xbox's Change in Strategy': Dishonored Dev Has Weeks to Save Itself
articles.content_orig:
While the future of former Xbox first-party devs like Double Fine and Undead Labs has already been determined, it’s been a while since we heard word from Arkane Lyon , the studio behind the acclaimed Dishonored games.
Now an article by Le Monde (paywalled) gives an insight into the struggles of the French studio, as it races to find a buyer before a 13th November deadline.
As you may recall, Microsoft was unable to close the studio immediately due to a consultation period demanded by French law. The Redmond firm is obligated to try to sell the studio, but a mandated three month deadline is now coming to a close.
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
The team has until 13th November to find new funding, otherwise the studio will be shuttered and around 217 jobs will be lost. According to the report, negotiations are ongoing.
Union representatives claim the team’s current project, Marvel’s Blade – which was announced in 2023 – is “nearing the end of production”. Spokespeople for the studio believe it will be a success if it sees the light of day.
But those same people blame Microsoft for its “disrespectful” treatment of the team.
“We are collateral victims of Xbox’s change in strategy,” one of the people said.
As alluded to above, Microsoft has already shuttered UK studio Ninja Theory , and offloaded various other teams like Compulsion Games et al.
It’s also in the process of reorganising its entire first-party operations, seemingly sunsetting Xbox Game Studios as it places its remaining teams under the umbrella of Bethesda and Activision. Its objective is to focus on big franchises like Fallout and Call of Duty .
The scary part is that the platform holder is not done yet: it’s cut over 1,800 jobs so far, but more redundancies are coming , as it aims to eliminate 3,200 roles overall.

articles.title_orig: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
articles.title_zh: Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus
articles.content_orig:
Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda
Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.
The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda , Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.
The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.
The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.
Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.
Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.
Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”
The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.
Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.
Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.
The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.
The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title_zh: Jared Kushner pushes back on report involving hacked phone, spies, billion-dollar transfer
articles.content_orig:
Jared Kushner is pushing back on a report involving a hacked iPhone, international spies and billion-dollar transfers from foreign governments.
An upcoming book by journalist Matthew Cole claims Kushner, who is President Trump's son-in-law, had access to more than $2 billion in "slush money funds" from Middle Eastern leaders in an attempt to influence U.S. foreign policy.
An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period.
Kushner and his legal team released fiery statements Thursday night categorically denying all accusations against him. Kushner said , "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." His attorney called them "false and defamatory" and said they intend to pursue legal action against those responsible, but did not specify whom.
The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government."
An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well.
According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it."
At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy.
The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank.
According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict.
The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit."
Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened."
"We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said.
"No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said.
CBS News reached out to the White House, which referred us to a statement from Steven Cheung, who is assistant to the president and White House director of communications.
Cheung said the "bull**** Vanity Fair article comes from a book that is complete fiction, and was fabricated from the warped mind of failed spy thriller writer."
"He presents no evidence or even a shred of documentation. Just mysterious words from unnamed sources," Cheung said on X.

articles.title_orig: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, state media say
articles.title_zh: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, state media say
articles.content_orig:
Six people were killed when gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, a government spokesperson has said.
Another 28 people were injured in the church in the village of Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.
The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing, in what government spokesperson Dr al-Momani Mohammad described as a "heinous attack".
Jordan's King Abdullah II said the authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties."
Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV.
He said two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes.
CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.
Two of the attackers are seen making their way onto what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.
Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid some chaotic scenes.
No-one has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.
A news briefing by interior ministry officials is expected shortly, and al-Momani has said the country's prime minister will chair a meeting of the Security Council to be attended by all ministers.
In his post on X, King Abdullah II offered his condolences to the families of the victims, writing: "Whoever imagines that the bullets of treachery can divide the ranks of Jordanians will fail in his endeavour before our steadfastness and unity."
Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media.
Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.
Such violence is rare in Jordan, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the country in the past.

China’s domestic online beauty sales are falling as C-beauty companies are ramping up export efforts and moving into international retail channels. The gap suggests a deliberate pivot from C-beauty toward overseas growth, targeting the categories and regions that K-beauty has spent the past decade winning over.
According to Jefferies’ China online beauty tracker , the country recorded a 6% year-on-year cosmetics sales decline in September 2026. Skin care fell 6.1%, while color cosmetics went down 5.2%.
However, at the same time, data from the Korea International Trade Association (KITA) shows China climbing from seventh place to fifth in global cosmetics exports. The trade body says China’s color cosmetics exports amount to nearly three times that of Korea’s.
C-beauty company Proya, meanwhile, has opened a European Innovation Center Laboratory in France and has announced it will begin selling across 400 Ulta Beauty stores in the US next month.
“This Europe Innovation Center Laboratory connects the European and Chinese ecosystems to draw on combined strengths and create new innovation capabilities,” says Hou Juncheng, founder and chairman of Proya Cosmetics.
The center is not the first bridge between Chinese and European beauty. French ingredient suppliers have been actively pursuing partnerships with Chinese cosmetics brands, and many Chinese perfumers train in France. The country’s Cosmetic Valley, meanwhile, has set up a Shanghai-based fragrance and cosmetics embassy to encourage collaboration between the two markets . Chinese beauty brands are expanding overseas, targeting markets where K-beauty has established a strong presence.
With color cosmetics exports already outpacing Korea’s and a growing foothold in US and European retail, C-beauty appears to be borrowing the playbook that got K-beauty onto global shelves.
The September figures from Jefferies’ tracker show many multinational beauty giants experiencing declining figures in China. L’Oréal fell 5%, Estée Lauder 8%, Procter & Gamble 20%, Shiseido 24%, and LVMH 26%.
Beiersdorf and Galderma were the only multinationals to grow, supported by their Nivea and Cetaphil brands. At the brand level, dermatological skin care like CeraVe and Cetaphil grew (35% and 58%, respectively), while Bobbi Brown fell 31%. Among domestic players, Mao Geping grew 26%, and Proya grew 1%.
As demand becomes increasingly selective, and derma-brands gain ground, Jefferies’ findings show skin care and color cosmetics accounting for over 80% of China’s beauty market. Both categories initially gave rise to K-beauty.
According to KITA, China’s cosmetic exports reached ₩8.14 trillion (US$6.1 billion) from January to July 2026, up 24% from ₩6.55 trillion (US$4.9 billion) a year earlier. The figures lifted China to fifth in global export rankings, behind France in the lead and South Korea in second place.
In color cosmetics, China has already overtaken Korea. Exports of lip and eye makeup, powders, and nail products totaled ₩1.88 trillion (US$1.41 billion) from January to July, about 2.9 times Korea’s ₩644.7 billion (US$484 million).
From January to July 2026, China’s lip makeup exports were 1.7 times Korea’s, and its eye makeup exports were 3.5 times. China’s exports grew 17% to 33% across all four color cosmetics categories (lip, eye, powders, and nail products), while Korea’s lip makeup and nail product exports fell 15% and 15.6%, respectively. Proya is expanding its international presence with a new research laboratory in France.
According to The Asia Business Daily, Kecia Steelman, CEO of Ulta Beauty, raised C-beauty during the company’s 2026 Q2 fiscal earnings call. She is quoted as saying, “[We are launching] Proya, the number one skin care brand in China. So it’s not just about K-Beauty anymore.”
Proya’s US launch will be the first time a Chinese premium skin care brand joins Ulta’s online and physical networks at the same time. The rollout is planned for November this year, and with it, Proya says it is “moving beyond mere product export to brand globalization.”
To expand, the company says, “brands must not only enter overseas markets but also earn a permanent place in consumers’ daily skin care regimens and secure a voice within elite global beauty narratives.”
Securing that voice, Proya has inaugurated its Europe Innovation Center Laboratory in France, with a 450 square meter site containing 76 pieces of equipment and seven dedicated researchers. The lab will focus on research and innovation in skin longevity, biology, biotechnology, and sustainable ingredients.
The lab will collaborate with the Hangzhou Longwu center in China, which handles formulation, ingredients, safety, and efficacy, and the Shanghai center, which works on hair care and the scalp microbiome.
Proya’s international push comes after its namesake brand, which accounts for around 70% of group revenue, posted a 7% sales decline in H1 2026. The drop was the company’s first after years of uninterrupted growth since its 2017 Shanghai listing. Jefferies says the brand returned to 1% growth in September, but the overseas expansion appears partly aimed at offsetting soft momentum.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive: Documents show German party’s scramble to request support after president’s 2016 election win and co-leader’s pursuit of Steve Bannon
A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade.
The trove reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.
The AfD became a home for anti-immigration voters after 1.2 million refugees arrived in Germany in 2015 and 2016. It entered the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, in 2017 with 12.6% of the vote , came second in the February 2025 federal election with 20.8% , and now leads national polls at about 30% . In September it won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and it is now trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the second world war.
Trump hailed the win in Saxony-Anhalt in a post on his Truth Social, concluding his message with a German version of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency monitors the party as a suspected rightwing extremist organisation , and state agencies classify five of its regional branches as confirmed extremist .
Its leader in the central Thuringia region, Björn Höcke, was convicted in 2024 of knowingly using a slogan of the SA, the Nazi party’s paramilitary wing. AfD politicians also attended a meeting with extremists at which a mass-deportation “masterplan” was discussed. Its 2025 election programme calls for lifting sanctions on Russia and repairing the Nord Stream gas pipelines programme . Nearly all of Germany’s other parties have kept a “firewall”, refusing to govern with it.
Media outlets including the Guardian have reported on the apparently friendly contacts between the party and the US state department during Trump’s second term.
The leaked documents show AfD officials quickly moving to requests for support from the White House on policy issues when he first won the 2016 election.
Others show a burgeoning political courtship between senior figures including the AfD’s now leader Alice Weidel and key Trump ideologue Steve Bannon.
The data, provided to reporters by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), covers more than 420,000 emails, along with documents and personnel records, from the party’s foundation in 2013 to the present, with most coming before 2019.
The AfD said in a statement on Monday that a hosting provider used by the party had been attacked at the end of September and that “only a few mailboxes” had been copied. It told the news agency dpa that most of those mailboxes had not been used for years, and party sources were quoted as saying the published material appeared to be authentic.
AfD figures praised Trump ahead of his first election in 2016, with then leader Frauke Petry calling him a “refreshingly alternative proposition” in the spring of 2016. On the day after Trump won the presidency, Petry said the victory was “encouraging for Germany and for Europe” .
The hacked documents reveal that in the wake of his election, the party scrambled to send an ingratiating telegram to the new president.
Mainstream German politicians greeted Trump’s election with skepticism. On 9 November 2016, then chancellor Angela Merkel offered Trump “close cooperation” only “on the basis of … values” including respect for human dignity “regardless of origin, skin colour, religion, gender, sexual orientation or political views”. The then defence minister Ursula von der Leyen called the result a “ huge shock ”. The next day the vice-chancellor, Sigmar Gabriel, reportedly called Trump the “forerunner of a new authoritarian and chauvinist international”, and he counted the AfD among its forces.
On 10 November, Petry emailed the party’s federal board proposing “an official and brief congratulatory telegram to the future US president”. German politics, she wrote, was “once again outdoing itself in politically unacceptable behaviour”; the AfD was “already perceived as the ones who don’t join in the majority howl of the political establishment” and, “as the only German party welcoming a new beginning in the US”, should say so officially.
Eleven of the board’s 13 members replied, all in favour. Current leader Weidel wrote “Yes:-)”. Beatrix von Storch, now deputy leader of the party’s Bundestag group, wrote: “Couldn’t be more of a yes.”
Board member Dirk Driesang added that Trump should also receive, “by post (?)”, the party’s manifesto in English.
The telegram went out on 11 November under Petry’s name, “on behalf of the federal board”, and was released to the press. It told the president-elect: “We are confident that you will readjust the transatlantic relationship and end the wars in Syria and Ukraine by mutual agreement with Russia.”
A second message, for the inauguration, was planned more carefully, and included a concrete request for a political favor. On 11 January 2017, Driesang asked for it to be put on the agenda of the board’s next conference call, “this time faster and better prepared”, and proposed adding a request: “Please support us in our efforts to remove the enemy-state clause from the UN charter.”
The “enemy state” clauses were written into the UN charter in 1945, and exempted action against “any state which during the second world war has been an enemy of any signatory” from the charter’s normal rules, so that the wartime allies could move against any “renewal of aggressive policy” by Germany, Japan or their allies. The general assembly declared them obsolete in 1995 and resolved to repeal them, but the text has never been amended, because changing the charter needs ratification by two-thirds of member states and all five permanent members of the security council.
No German party currently defends the clauses, but the Bundestag’s own research service wrote in 2017 that international lawyers unanimously regard the clauses as having no practical relevance . On the German right, however, the clauses are totemic , and viewed as a limitation on German sovereignty. The AfD’s Bundestag group demanded its deletion in a 2020 motion that called it a “relic of the past” which “indirectly designates Germany an ‘enemy state’”, and every other party voted it down .
AfD’s federal board adopted the enemy state request on its call of 16 January, according to the federal office’s record of the decision contained in the leaked documents.
When the office circulated an English draft on 19 January, Georg Pazderski, then the party’s Berlin leader and a member of its federal board, objected to the tone and to the request for support: “You don’t address the president as Mr Trump, he is Mr President. Otherwise a bit wordy and flowery. I stand by it: the enemy-state clause doesn’t belong in this letter at all. You don’t do that in a letter of congratulation. It looks like a begging letter.”
Driesang replied at 6.16 the next morning: “Personally I of course find the style appropriate, otherwise I wouldn’t have written it that way.”
The office also wanted to know how the telegram should reach Trump: “directly to Trump’s campaign team … or through official diplomatic channels (e.g. the US embassy in Berlin)?”
André Poggenburg, then the party’s leader in Saxony-Anhalt, answered: “all available channels.”
The text released on the afternoon of 20 January, signed by Petry and her then co-leader Jörg Meuthen, kept the request. articles.title_orig: French authorities deploy 70,000 officers for Saturday protests; Louvre and other museums closed
articles.title_zh: French authorities deploy 70,000 officers for Saturday protests; Louvre and other museums closed
articles.content_orig:
Move follows some of the worst street violence in years on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend
France will deploy about 70,000 police around the country on Saturday as the government seeks to prevent more civil unrest after some of the worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend.
The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on ⁠Friday ⁠the security forces would include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism operations and hostage rescues, adding that there had been social media calls for violence from “ultra-left” groups.
“We are not talking about ⁠a peaceful, friendly demonstration,” Nuñez ​told reporters after a meeting of senior ministers and officials chaired by the president, Emmanuel Macron. “We ​are ​ready tomorrow ​to be ‌extremely firm ​and ​not tolerate anything.”
Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has caught it off guard six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.
Largely peaceful demonstrations were hijacked by groups of determined rioters, degenerating into rampant violence and extensive looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities. In Limoges, the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed.
“We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all who commit violence,” Nuñez said, adding that besides 10,000 more police, the operation would include water cannon, armoured vehicles, mounted police, helicopters and drones.
Demonstrations are expected in several other countries this weekend, triggered by a broader, continent-wide wave of discontent over declining public services, housing affordability, public sector budget cuts and the spiralling cost of living.
Protests over related grievances have been called for Saturday in Milan, Rome and Turin in Italy; in Vienna, Austria; and in Madrid, Barcelona and other cities in Spain, as well as in Lisbon and Porto in Portugal, Dublin in Ireland and Tirana in Albania.
Protests are expected across France on Saturday, although several cities have banned demonstrations or forced them to change their planned routes to protect shops and public buildings, and forecast heavy rain and high winds could dampen turnout.
The centres of Lyon and some other large cities will be off-limits to protesters, while authorities in Paris authorised a union march along a limited route in the east of the capital between the Places de la Bastille and Nation that will avoid the city centre.
But requests for rallies in Paris organised by France’s main student union, UNEF, and the gilets jaunes movement, whose nationwide protests rocked France in 2018 and which plans 600 small-scale events around France on Saturday, were refused.
UNEF said its rallies, which grew from high school protests last month against teacher shortages and dilapidated facilities, would go ahead regardless. Several of the best-known cultural institutions in Paris, including the Louvre, said they would close on Saturday.
Authorities in Marseille had also banned all protests, but announced on Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis”. It will be the only authorised protest in the southern Bouches-du-Rhône department.
Unionists and opposition leaders have criticised the government for refusing to allow more rallies on Saturday, a decision being challenged in court in several cities. Marylise Léon of the CFDT union federation accused Macron of an abuse of authority.

“It’s ​counterproductive because there is a lot ​of anger and a demand to be considered and to be listened to,” Léon, the CFDT’s general secretary, told TF1 TV. “It’s not for the president to decide who can legitimately protest.”
La France Insoumise, the radical left party of Jean-Luc Mélenchon, said the government had “crossed the lines that separate a democracy from an authoritarian and police state”, adding that the bans would only “generate more chaos”.
Adding to the tensions, the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner for next spring’s presidential elections, is due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orléans, drawing thousands of supporters – and leftwing, anti-racist opponents.
Nuñez was due to visit the city on Friday to “inspect the security arrangements” at the request of the prime minister’s office. The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 217 people – half of them first-time offenders – had been jailed since Saturday.
On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency”, saying gangs of rioters had been mainly responsible for the looting but the worst violence was caused by “ultra-left” groups seeking to “bring down the republic”.
Further stoking disquiet, one person was killed and four others injured – including a 12-year-old girl – in ⁠a shooting in the town of Trappes, west of Paris, on Friday in an attack that police said could have been racially motivated.

US stocks were mixed on Friday as worries over the AI trade lingered, following this week's steep sell-off in Tech ( XLK ) that triggered a flight to bonds.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 1.1%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 0.2%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) edged 0.3% higher after semiconductors and Big Tech sold off on Thursday.
The 10-year Treasury (^ TNX ) yield held below the 5% threshold as investors flocked to bonds.
The AI trade sank on Thursday as concerns over rising financing costs and a potential slowdown in capex weighed on already-battered neocloud stocks like CoreWeave ( CRWV ). AI chip giants Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD ( SPCX ) also retreated, along with other infrastructure plays.
Shares of this week's earnings headliners, SpaceX ( SPCX ), Tesla ( TSLA ), and Meta ( META ), stabilized in Friday trading after declining in the previous session.
Oil prices remained near a five-month high amid fears of escalating tensions in the Middle East, with Brent crude ( BZ=F ) hovering near $111 per barrel and West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) climbing to $102 per barrel.
Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre reports:
Apple ( AAPL ) is taking Wall Street's crown back from Nvidia — for the fifth time.
Apple briefly topped Nvidia in market value on Friday. It's a move Apple has made before, and it has rarely stuck.
Apple and Nvidia ( NVDA ) are each worth about $5.1 trillion, and the gap between them was less than 1% at Thursday's close. The flip came alongside a record run for Apple's stock and the day the tech giant's $1,999 iPhone Duo hit stores , capping a battle investors had been watching all morning. Nvidia has since moved back into the lead.
Shares of American Express ( AXP ) fell 3% Friday after the credit card giant delivered third quarter results and said it plans to eliminate roughly 5% of its workforce globally as part of a restructuring effort.
American Express CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts the cuts are part of a restructuring effort to make the company a "more agile and efficient organization." As part of the effort, the firm recognized a $336 million restructuring charge in the third quarter.
A company spokeswoman told Yahoo Finance the reduction will eliminate 3,500 roles globally.
Squeri added that earlier this year he asked senior executives to find ways to cut corporate bloat across the company in order to refocus on American Express' biggest priorities.
Earlier this month, federal bank regulators fined the credit card giant $350 million over widespread failures in its anti-money laundering controls.
In the third quarter, American Express reported revenue climbed 9% to $14.5 billion from a year ago while adjusted earnings per share rose 13% to $4.68. Analysts were expecting $14.8 billion in revenue.
Yahoo Finance's Daniel Howley reports:
Meta ( META ) stock pared losses in premarket action Friday, following a dismal Thursday trading session. Shares of the social media giant plunged 7%, despite reporting better-than-anticipated Q3 revenue on Wednesday as AI bubble fears reemerged across Wall Street.
Investors have been pulling back on semiconductor and other AI stocks across the board on questions about whether massive investments in AI data centers will pay off in the long run.
Meta raised the lower end of its capital expenditure estimates to between $135 billion and $145 billion from $130 billion and $145 billion. The company also has $825 billion in various spending commitments related to cloud capacity arrangements, energy service agreements, and consumer hardware products.
US stocks opened lower as investors reassessed technology stocks following the Nasdaq Composite's worst day since June.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 1%, while those for the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) dropped 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) decreased 0.3% after semiconductors and Big Tech sold off on Thursday.
At Friday's open, major indices are on pace for a clear split in weekly performance after all three traded lower on Thursday.
The Nasdaq is on pace for its second consecutive week of losses, while the Dow is poised for its third straight week of gains. The S&P 500 is hovering near the flatline for the week.
Meanwhile, oil prices rose early Friday as momentum builds around renewed tensions in the Middle East conflict.
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports:
Don't expect SpaceX ( SPCX ) to surprise investors like Meta ( META ) did this week by announcing it would issue a new class of nonvoting stock to help fund its AI build-out.
"Importantly, in our discussion w/management, SPCX also said that it is not considering raising equity," JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth wrote in a new post-earnings note on Friday. "Capital requirements are front and center across the market, and SPCX indicated it has a number of available pools of capital on the debt side."
SpaceX gave investors a taste of what could be to come on the debt funding front in its earnings report this week.
Yahoo Finance' Brian Sozzi reports:

articles.title_zh: People are fixing their TV OSes with Claude
articles.content_orig:
Users are getting fed up with the barrage of ads and data tracking on TVs and are looking to AI vibe coding for the answer.
Users are getting fed up with the barrage of ads and data tracking on TVs and are looking to AI vibe coding for the answer.
Vibe coding has reached TVs. Social media is awash with posts from people using LLMs and open-source tools to remove ads and tracking, trim bloat so the OS runs faster, and even completely change the look and organization of their homescreens. While a lot of it is fun — one user turned their TV homescreen into a Pokémon town — I think there’s a level of frustration behind it, too. And TV companies should take notice.
Several vibe-coded TV-debloating projects exploded in popularity over the weekend. Cleanyourtv (known as tv-vibehack until the 19th), tv-detox , and dumbtv all claim to accomplish similar things — remove sponsored ads, debloat the TV so it runs faster, and block unwanted data collection that tracks what you’re watching — without hacking, or rooting, the TV. By default, they all also replace the TV’s built-in app launcher with simpler ones. Many users are going a step further and vibe-coding their own replacement launchers, like the Pokémon one below.
Most of the projects we’ve seen so far focus on TVs that run on Android and Google TV operating systems (such as TCL, Hisense, Sony, and older Amazon Fire products), using existing developer modes and the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to tweak settings and apply (and remove) packages. According to the GitHub pages, they can also work with some Fire TV products that use a custom fork of Android (although likely not on the new Vega-based Fire TV Sticks). Because they use built-in developer tools, they don’t require root access or firmware hacking, and they’re reversible. Even projects that totally change the look of the interface just use Android’s ability to install custom launchers — in many cases with an assist from Claude Code or a similar tool to create the new launcher, too.
As Verge friend Chris Person notes in his Aftermath post , none of this requires AI. These projects take advantage of capabilities that already exist in Android, and in some cases reinvent the wheel. Android debloating programs that use ADB have been around for years, and so have replacement launchers that make Google TV OS look like Apple TV . AI just made the process easier and faster.
There’s nothing similar available for Samsung’s Tizen OS or LG’s webOS, apart from rooting the TV, which is a whole different level of hacking and device control. While there’s a webOS vibe hack for LG TVs that’s based on cleanyourtv, it doesn’t really do the same thing, essentially streaming the Apple TV-like launcher from an always-on device on the same network. They also won’t work for Roku or Vizio’s SmartCast.
These projects, or any OS vibe coding someone might attempt, won’t necessarily stop all data collection. A good basic rule is that if the TV is connected to the internet, it’s collected at least some data. Dumbtv blocks certain manufacturer and ad partner addresses your TV sends data to, but since it’s usually encrypted during transit, knowing what exactly gets sent is impossible. The data blocking is similar to what you can do with Pi-hole to block malicious DNS requests on your network.
TVs have increasingly become a means for companies to gather viewing data and serve up ads. By using automatic content recognition (ACR) and digital fingerprinting, manufacturers are able to know what content you’re watching, send that information to their ad partners, and then display targeted ads on the TV.
ACR isn’t just used for ads, though. It allows companies to measure audience metrics, and it can feed show recommendations based on what you’ve watched. It’s important to note that users need to agree to ACR tracking, and there are ways to opt out of it after the fact in a TV’s menus (although those options are not always easy to find). There are also options in most menus — again, usually buried — for turning off targeted ads.
But even after doing that, there’s always concern that companies still collect some amount of your data and use it in ways you might not be comfortable with. Whether or not it’s true does little to assuage those fears. The weekend of vibe coding, on the other hand, is a way for people to try and take control of their TVs to get the user experience they want.
There are also dangers to vibe-coding your TV. One person who tried to vibe-hack a Samsung TV with Claude bricked it. The only way to fully avoid ACR, ads, or any type of data collection is to never connect it to the internet. A firmware download to a USB stick can apply critical updates instead of Wi-Fi or Ethernet. If you still want to stream content, a streaming device that doesn’t use ACR , like an Apple TV 4K (grab a last-generation model before the expensive new one replaces it), is an option. But any streaming requires sharing some amount of your data with someone to function properly.
The biggest takeaway from the vibe-coding weekend is that the current state of TV OSes has people fed up. Most people aren’t going to stop watching TV anytime soon, but the experience needs to improve. The ads, the data collection, and the cluttered layouts are too aggravating. AI now allows anyone to code their own solution, and it’s only going to get easier. If TV manufacturers don’t take note and make changes, there’s a chance that users will make the changes for them.

articles.title_orig: ASUS ProArt P16 Review: A Sleek Showcase For NVIDIA's RTX Spark
articles.title_zh: ASUS ProArt P16 Review: A Sleek Showcase For NVIDIA's RTX Spark
articles.content_orig:
But it's really only meant for AI fanatics.
ASUS's first laptop featuring an RTX Spark chip confirms what I originally thought: NVIDIA's new PC platform really isn't meant for everyone. The ProArt P16 is yet another one of the company's premium notebooks focused on power-hungry creators — except this time, it's running NVIDIA's first major PC chipset, instead of an Intel or AMD processor. Outside of the hype from Microsoft and NVIDIA, who are positioning RTX spark as a complete "reinvention" of the PC, the ProArt P16 is simply a nice laptop. It's particularly appealing if you're running local AI models, since it can squeeze up to 128GB of RAM into a relatively slim case.
The downsides? It's incredibly expensive, with a starting price of $2,800 and staggering increases as you add more RAM. (Spoiler: Our review model costs $7,000, mostly thanks to its 128GB of RAM.) And even though the ASUS P16 can play games well, you're paying far more here than you would for a dedicated gaming laptop.
Much like the ProArt PX13 we reviewed earlier this year, the ProArt P16 shows just how far ASUS has come with premium laptops. It sports a beautiful and sturdy aluminum case, a wonderfully bright 16-inch OLED screen, a luxuriously-spaced keyboard and a similarly enormous haptic touchpad. It's MacBook-esque in its sleekness, except it has an ASUS badge. The ProArt P16 is even lighter than the 16-inch MacBook Pro, clocking in at 3.9 pounds, compared to Apple's 4.7 pounds.
From afar, the ASUS P16 doesn't look particularly special. But peek under the hood, and you'll quickly see what makes it different. It's powered entirely by NVIDIA's RTX Spark system-on-a-chip, which brings together a 20-core Arm CPU, a modern Blackwell GPU, and, as I mentioned, up to 128GB of unified memory. If that sounds familiar, it's because it's very similar to the way Apple has configured its M-series chips, which was the main reason we've adored that company's computers since 2020.
Unlike Apple's chip revamp, RTX Spark won't completely replace x86 hardware from Intel and AMD. You can think of it as a new fork of PC design aimed squarely at AI researchers and enthusiasts. RTX Spark is also meant to coexist with Qualcomm's Snapdragon X chips, which use a similar Arm-based design for entry-level and midrange systems.
As I've previously reported , there's a good chance that, despite a niche audience, RTX Spark will likely be a win for Windows PCs in general. Competition is always good for consumers — with NVIDIA planting its flag in the Windows world, you can certainly bet that AMD, Intel and Qualcomm will up their game with future hardware. Unfortunately, RTX Spark likely won't help PCs revert back to their pre-AI boom pricing. It's yet another memory-hungry platform at a time when AI has already driven RAM prices through the roof.
At least NVIDIA and PC makers are trying to stuff in all of the pro-level features RTX Spark owners may want. In addition to the hardware I've mentioned above, the ASUS P16 also squeezes in just about every port you'd need, including three USB-C connections, USB Type A, HDMI, a headphone jack and a full-sized SD card reader. Ethernet would be nice, but that's become a true rarity in thinner, pro-grade laptops.
Using the ASUS P16 with RTX Spark reminded me of the first time I turned on a MacBook Pro with an M-series chip: Everything about it feels lightning fast. I was up and running in no time, and I felt unstoppable as I downloaded several massive files simultaneously to start my benchmarking process. But of course, for a $7,000 system with 128GB of RAM, it damn well better feel speedy.
I'll admit, I was a bit surprised by the ASUS P16's initial benchmark scores: Its PCMark 10 (Applications) figure was 3,000 points lower than the ultra-slim ASUS A16 I tested earlier this year, which was powered by a Snapdragon X2 Elite chip. The RTX Spark system also lagged behind slightly in Geekbench 6's single-threaded CPU test, which is a sign that Qualcomm's chips just have more capable CPUs.
But really, the star of the RTX Spark's design is its GPU, NPU and unified memory, and those all stood out in other tests. The ASUS P16 RTX Spark was 4,700 points higher than the MacBook Pro with M5 Max in Geekbench 6's GPU benchmark, which tests overall graphics performance. The ProArt P16 also scored 3,895 points in UL Procyon's AI Computer Vision 2 benchmark, compared to 3,267 points from that same MacBook. Its 1,519 score in Procyon's AI Image Generation test was also 600 points higher than Apple's. Those Procyon benchmarks all clearly benefitted from the RTX Spark chip' s beefy graphics power.
Beyond benchmarks, the ASUS P16 was able to run OpenClaw and the large Qwen3.8 27B model, which alone takes up 42GB of RAM, while still leaving me with a ton of RAM for other tasks. At the same time, I was even able to play Control: Resonant and Cyberpunk 2077 at high quality settings without breaking a sweat. Sure, the fans sounded like they were about to lift the P16 off my desk, but there was never any noticeable slowdown in performance.
NVIDIA has previously said that the RTX Spark's graphics hardware is about on-par with the RTX 5070 mobile GPU, while also drawing much less power, and that held true in my testing. I was able to play Control Resonant at 70 fps while rendering the game in 1,440p with "ultra" graphics settings, ray-tracing set to medium and 4x frame generation. That's a game where the overall fidelity matters more than a triple-digit framerate, but I could get the ProArt P16 to 120 fps by lowering the graphics settings.
While I didn't have much trouble running other games, including Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Gears of War: E-Day , there's a chance you'll have trouble with some titles. Since RTX Spark is based on an Arm CPU, it has to rely on Microsoft's Prism emulator to handle most games. That introduces an immediate performance drop, as well as potential issues. There are native Arm64 builds for popular titles like Fortnite , DOTA 2, Marvel Rivals and the upcoming World of Warcraft: Forever , so there's a chance that compatibility concerns will melt away in a few years. But if you don't want to worry about emulation troubles at all, you're better off with a standard gaming laptop running an Intel or AMD chip.
There are also similar compatibility concerns for older Windows software in general, though I didn't encounter any weirdness during my testing. The whole Windows on Arm experience received a huge upgrade when Copilot+ systems launched two years ago, and since then, it seems like Microsoft has worked to make its x86 emulation even more seamless.
The ProArt P16's 16-inch "Lumina Pro" OLED screen was perfect for Control Resonant : It was able to show off dark black levels and extreme contrast in darker environments, but it also seared my eyeballs at times with its peak 1,600-nit luminance. It's definitely one of the brightest OLED screens I've seen on a laptop, and it directly competes with Apple's Mini LED MacBook Pro displays, which also top out at 1,600 nits. That extreme brightness also made the ProArt P16 perfect for getting work done outside in the sun, as I try to eke out every bit of warmth I can before winter arrives.
I was similarly impressed by every other aspect of the ASUS ProArt P16. Its wide keyboard and luscious key depth made typing a dream, and it also has one of the best haptic touchpads I've ever seen on a Windows PC. While it would have been nice to have a quad-speaker setup, which has become increasingly common in large premium laptops, the ProArt P16's dual speakers still sounded solid. They also offer a bit of spatial audio support, thanks to Dolby Atmos.
The only major downside to the ProArt P16, like most jet-black PCs, is that it's a horrendous fingerprint magnet. Marks start appearing the instant you touch it, and heaven forbid you eat anything oily while using it. It takes just a few minutes for the P16 to start looking like a gross mess, and

Flávio Bolsonaro—the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro—and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to a runoff. Another key race was decided that day: In congressional elections, right-wing parties triumphed and are expected to hold at least 45 of 81 seats in the Senate.
Brazil’s Senate confirms (and can remove) justices on the Supreme Court, whose expanding judicial reach has made it a central arbiter of Brazilian democracy. Decisions by the bench could yet shape the outcome of the runoff, set for Oct. 25.
On Sept. 15, Chief Justice Edson Fachin convened a televised session to decide whether Justice Alexandre de Moraes—who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution and is reviled by the far right—should be investigated by the Federal Police. (Brazilian law requires courts to authorize investigations into their own members.) The justices never reached a decision: They split on a procedural motion, with Moraes voting on his own case, before Justice Flávio Dino asked for up to 90 days to study the file. That clock runs until mid-December—well after the runoff.
The case swirling around Moraes stems from the collapse last year of Banco Master , a midsize Brazilian lender. The scandal—like the Operation Car Wash investigation of the mid-2010s—has ensnared many members of Brazil’s political and business elite. Federal Police hope to examine whether Moraes improperly assisted Master’s controlling shareholder, Daniel Vorcaro, and whether that conduct was connected to a legal services contract between Master and Moraes’s wife’s law firm. Moraes denies wrongdoing. He has not been charged with a crime.
The scandal has become a hot topic on the campaign trail, and one likely to benefit Flávio. By putting off a decision on whether to investigate Moraes, the Supreme Court has handed Flávio a rallying cry, left Lula defending an institution that he has no plan to reform, and made the new right-wing Senate the arbiter of the court’s future.
Prior to its collapse, Banco Master held only 0.57 percent of Brazil’s banking assets. But its unique business model made it significant.
The bank sold certificates of deposit paying up to 140 percent of the interbank benchmark rate, far above what large banks offered. It leaned on the Credit Guarantee Fund, an insurer financed by member banks that covers up to about $49,000 per investor. (Although privately funded, the fund operates under government-set rules, and eligible banks are required to join and contribute.) This allowed Master to raise money without investors scrutinizing what it bought, including illiquid assets and credit portfolios that, according to investigators, lacked adequate backing.
Master also drew on public money. Banco de Brasília (BRB), a lender controlled by the government of the Federal District, bought Master’s credit portfolios. In March 2025, BRB agreed to buy 58 percent of the bank. The Central Bank blocked the deal that September and shut Master down on Nov. 18. The Credit Guarantee Fund repaid roughly $7.5 billion to about 800,000 savers, so taxpayers did not cover that bill. But BRB’s losses fall on the public: Federal Police found that BRB paid about $1.4 billion for Master portfolios before finishing at least one of its required risk assessments. BRB has since asked the district government for fresh capital.
Master’s reach went beyond finance: Vorcaro told police that he had friends in all branches of government, and the case has drawn in politicians across the political spectrum.
Ibaneis Rocha, the former Federal District governor, called the occasion of the proposed acquisition “a day of celebration,” and he left office in March to run for the Senate. He dropped out of the race in July, after the BRB president whom he had appointed was jailed.
Police say Master’s staff drafted an amendment to a proposed constitutional reform to quadruple the Credit Guarantee Fund’s per-depositor coverage that Sen. Ciro Nogueira, Jair Bolsonaro’s former chief of staff, introduced in Congress in 2024. Police have also said that Nogueira received monthly payments of up to roughly $98,000 from Vorcaro and figures associated with Master. Nogueira denies wrongdoing.
The Supreme Court took over the Master investigation because it involves members of Congress, who in Brazil can only be investigated with the Supreme Court’s authorization—and tried by the court itself. Justice Dias Toffoli was initially assigned to the case. He stepped aside in February after police flagged that funds managed by Vorcaro’s brother-in-law had a stake in a resort from a company partly owned by Toffoli and his brothers. Toffoli’s office has said he never had a friendship with Vorcaro.
The case was then reassigned to Justice André Mendonça, a Jair Bolsonaro appointee.
Brazil’s far-right presidential hopeful wants to step up ties with Washington. But like his father, he would struggle to spurn Beijing.
Slow growth and corruption have dogged the right and the left.
The scandal has reached both presidential campaigns, though not in the same way. Flávio’s exposure is direct: In May, Intercept Brasil published audio of him asking Vorcaro for money to finish Dark Horse , a biopic about his father. Flávio first denied any connection to Vorcaro, then acknowledged seeking the sponsorship, which he described as legitimate private investment.
Records from Brazil’s financial intelligence unit trace about $12.3 million from a Vorcaro-linked company to a Texas fund that managed the film’s money and is run by an ally of Flávio’s brother Eduardo, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to sanction Moraes. Police documents do not link the money to Flávio’s personal accounts. In July, Mendonça authorized a formal investigation into possible corruption, money laundering, and currency evasion connected to the financing of Dark Horse . Neither brother has been charged in connection with the film’s financing.
Lula’s exposure is indirect. He is not implicated in wrongdoing, according to tax records reviewed by Reuters, though he met with Vorcaro in December 2024. This June, police executed search warrants targeting Sen. Jaques Wagner, who was then the Senate leader, on suspicion that he had advanced Master’s interests in exchange for benefits for relatives. Wagner, a member of Lula’s Workers’ Party, denies wrongdoing. He has since resigned from his leadership post.
For Lula, the larger liability is Moraes. Much of the Brazilian electorate places the justice and the president in the same camp—never mind that Moraes was appointed by right-wing former President Michel Temer.
